newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces new test as deputies debate budget.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces new test as deputies debate budget.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, under pressure to resign for health reasons, faced a new test on Friday in a parliamentary debate on whether to approve his government's 1997 budget.

His bitter foes the communists, who launched an initiative this week to oust him, said their support for the budget would depend on the government's readiness to pay huge wage and pension arrears swiftly to millions of Russians.
Yeltsin kept a low profile as proceedings began in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament.
The Kremlin press service said the 65-year-old president met Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais at the Gorky-9 residence outside Moscow where he is recovering from pneumonia.
It gave no details but said Yeltsin was also doing paperwork, including preparing a speech which he is expected to make to deputies from both houses of parliament next month.
A brief visit to the Kremlin on Wednesday, less than two full days after he left hospital, failed to end doubts over Yeltsin's health and his ability to rule.
The Duma debated a motion on Wednesday on trying to oust Yeltsin and discussions are set to continue next month.
Yeltsin, who was re-elected last July, was out of the Kremlin for most of the second half of last year with heart problems and he had a bypass operation on November 5.
The communists, the largest force in the Duma, had another chance to attack Yeltsin and the government of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in the budget debate.
"It looks as though there are going to be some serious fights and long discussions," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Viktor Ilyukhin, a senior communist deputy, as saying.
Deputies have approved three readings of the budget. The government, facing huge economic problems, has agreed to raise spending in several areas in efforts to win over the opposition.
The economy would keep running if the Duma voted against the budget but rejection would be another snub to Yeltsin, hampering many of his economic plans.

Parliamentarians have also put pressure on Yeltsin this week by criticising Chubais and Boris Berezovsky, deputy secretary of the Security Council which is negotiating with separatist leaders in rebel Chechnya.
Security was stepped up in Chechnya in Friday before Monday's presidential and parliamentary elections in the region, but officials said trouble could not be ruled out.
Russia sent troops into Chechnya in December 1994 but has now pulled them out after failing to put down resistance in 21 months of fighting over the region's independence demands.
Yeltsin also faces major foreign policy challenges this year, including a dispute with NATO over its plans to take in new members from eastern and central Europe.
U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott met Chernomyrdin in Moscow to prepare for the prime minister's trip to the United States next month, Russian news agencies said.

NATO sources in Brussels said Talbott had also brought with him new proposals for a deal cutting the huge U.S. advantage in sea-based strategic nuclear missiles as part of efforts to win Russian support for NATO's plans to expand eastwards.
